strengths: Introduces a challenging and practically relevant benchmark for fine-grained visual reasoning on high-resolution transit maps, covering 30 cities across 13 countries and multiple languages.
Provides a semi-automated dataset construction pipeline and a two-level evaluation framework that attempts to assess both answer correctness and route quality, going beyond simple accuracy.
Conducts a broad evaluation of 15 MLLMs, including open- and closed-source, base and reasoning variants, plus a masked-visual-input study that gives useful evidence about visual grounding.
Includes qualitative error analysis and case studies that identify recurring failure modes such as visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, refusal, and city/language effects.
Addresses ethical and licensing considerations and indicates plans to release code and dataset sources.
weaknesses: The central claim that open-source base models outperform reasoning variants (and the reverse for closed-source) is not supported by controlled comparisons: the models differ in family, scale, and training data, and only one open-source pair (Kimi-VL-A3B Instruct/Thinking) is actually matched.

The proposed map score is not clearly specified and does not independently measure answer quality: Algorithm 2 contains an ambiguous/erroneous normalization line and a correctness bonus, so quality and correctness are entangled; if taken literally, the printed formula is invalid.

The benchmark is relatively small (1,008 QA pairs; 312 test samples), and some difficulty buckets contain very few examples (e.g., one sample for hard-middle), making per-bucket results noisy and limiting statistical reliability.
No human performance baseline, inter-annotator agreement, or statistical significance tests are provided, making it difficult to interpret model scores or claim meaningful differences between models.

Quality ground truth relies on Google/Gaode API reference routes, which may not cover all valid routes and may change over time; valid alternative routes not returned by the APIs could be unfairly penalized.

Reproducibility is limited because the transit map images are not redistributed (only source links are given), and details of the MLLM-based extraction and manual correction process are insufficiently described.

Novelty over existing map/spatial reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MapEval, CityBench, GeoNav, PlanAgent) is incremental; the paper does not convincingly establish a uniquely challenging evaluation beyond using transit maps.

Potential data contamination is not adequately ruled out: publicly available transit maps and station names may appear in MLLM pretraining data, and masked-image experiments do not fully eliminate the influence of prior knowledge.

The claimed 'counterintuitive pattern' is overstated given confounded model comparisons, small effect sizes, and lack of uncertainty estimates; some city-level and difficulty-level conclusions remain speculative.

strengths: Introduces ReasonMap, a benchmark targeting fine-grained visual understanding and spatial reasoning over high-resolution transit maps, an underexplored but practically relevant and structured visual domain that existing benchmarks (MathVQA, MMMU, MathVerse, V*-Bench, etc.) do not adequately cover.

Dataset construction is careful and semi-automated: 1,008 human-verified QA pairs spanning 30 cities in 13 countries, with manual correction of line/stop annotations, reference-route verification, and explicit difficulty balancing across maps and questions.

Proposes a two-level evaluation framework that separates answer correctness (accuracy) from answer quality (a proposed map score), enabling more nuanced assessment of route-level and endpoint consistency, via-stop counts, and set overlap.

Comprehensive benchmarking across 15 MLLMs including both base and reasoning variants, complemented by an error analysis with qualitative case studies and a visual-input-masking experiment that yields actionable insights (e.g., open-source reasoning variants underperforming base models; reliance on prior knowledge without visual input).
Reasonable reproducibility: map sources are enumerated, model licenses documented, code release stated, and evaluation algorithms (Algorithms 1 and 2) provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is modest: 1,008 QA pairs with only 312 samples in the test set. Many difficulty buckets are extremely small (Figure 3 reports as few as 1 sample for hard-middle), which undermines the statistical reliability of the reported accuracies and of the central base-vs-reasoning conclusions.

The map score and difficulty-aware weighting introduce several arbitrary design choices (caps at 10/20/40, fixed bonus points, weight matrix from 1.0 to 3.0) with little justification, sensitivity analysis, or ablation, so the metric's robustness is unclear.

Explanations for the headline 'counterintuitive' finding (open-source reasoning models underperforming their base counterparts, opposite for closed-source) are largely speculative (RL biasing output distributions, broader knowledge coverage), and the paper itself acknowledges the closed-source comparison may not be fair; no direct experiment isolates the cause.

The masked-visual-input study is limited to a subset of models and may conflate refusal behavior, format errors, and genuine reliance on prior knowledge, since invalid/unparsable responses are zeroed out rather than analyzed separately.

Generalization of the conclusions is untested: the benchmark covers a single type of structured diagram (transit maps), and the authors acknowledge geographic/linguistic coverage is not exhaustive; it is unclear whether findings transfer to other fine-grained visual reasoning settings.

As a benchmark contribution, the reported study is essentially correlational; it does not probe deeper into why fine-grained visual grounding fails or provide training/evaluation methodology advances beyond the metric design.

strengths: Targets a genuine and underexplored gap: fine-grained visual reasoning over high-resolution, information-dense structured diagrams (transit maps). The authors correctly note that existing benchmarks (MathVista, MMMU, MathVerse, VisuLogic, VGRP-Bench, etc.) do not systematically evaluate this capability, and Table 1 makes the distinction (avg resolution 5,839 x 5,449, training set, step evaluation, multilingual) reasonably clear.

Dataset construction is thoughtfully designed with human verification: 30 cities across 13 countries, manual route verification, standardized stop/transfer annotation, and a semi-automated pipeline (Figure 2) that is described as extensible. Quality control covers correctness, diversity, and difficulty balance, which lends credibility to the annotations.

The two-level evaluation framework is a meaningful design choice. Separating correctness (Algorithm 1, endpoint/segment/transfer consistency) from quality (map score, Algorithm 2, route/endpoint matching, via-stop count and via-stop IoU) allows finer-grained assessment than a single accuracy number, and the difficulty-aware weighting is a reasonable attempt to reflect task complexity.

The benchmarking study is broad and informative: 15 MLLMs spanning base and reasoning variants, open- and closed-source, multiple families, plus a no-visual-input ablation (Table 3). The finding that open-source base models outperform their reasoning counterparts while the reverse holds for closed-source models is a useful and somewhat surprising signal, and the masking experiment gives evidence that the tasks require genuine visual grounding rather than textual priors alone.

Qualitative analysis (Figures 5, A1-A3) is concrete and useful: it categorizes visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, and refusal, and shows interpretable failure modes (e.g., misidentifying Line 9 vs. Line 16, English vs. Chinese stop names affecting recognition). This adds diagnostic value beyond raw scores.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: code is released under MIT, all map sources are listed (Table A1), evaluation algorithms and question templates are provided in the appendix, and model licenses are documented.
The paper is clearly written and well-organized; figures and tables communicate the pipeline, difficulty distribution, and cross-city patterns effectively.
weaknesses: The dataset is small for a benchmark: 1,008 QA pairs total and only 312 samples in the test split. Several difficulty buckets in Figure 3 have very few samples (e.g., hard-middle has 1 sample, hard-easy 7, middle-middle 23), so per-bucket accuracy and map-score comparisons are likely noisy. The paper itself notes the 100% accuracy at hard-middle is an artifact of a single sample, but does not fully address how this affects the conclusions.

Question diversity is limited. All questions are template-generated, and effectively probe route identification, via-stop counting, and via-stop enumeration. The 'short' template mainly requires naming lines and endpoints, and the two 'long' templates only differ in counting vs. enumerating via stops. This narrow scope may under-represent the breadth of fine-grained spatial reasoning the benchmark claims to assess.

The map-score formulation in Algorithm 2 is underspecified and appears problematic. The line `map_score <- map_score + 10/map_score + 20` (and the analogous short/long capping logic) is mathematically odd and depends on the running value of map_score in a way that is not justified; it is unclear whether this is a typo or intended. Similarly, the cap values (10/20/40) and the bonus structure are not motivated. Since quality is a headline contribution, this reduces confidence in the metric.

The difficulty labeling for question difficulty is defined solely by number of transfers (0 = easy, 1 = medium, >1 = hard), which is a coarse proxy and may not align with actual reasoning difficulty; the paper provides little validation that this correlates with model error or human difficulty.

The two evaluation ground truths come from different sources (Map Metadata for correctness vs. Google/Gaode API routes for quality), and routes that cannot be visually traced are discarded. This is reasonable but the residual risk of API routes not matching the visually rendered map (e.g., due to map version, express/local variants, service hours) is not quantified, which could introduce label noise.

The central 'counterintuitive' finding (base > reasoning for open-source, reverse for closed-source) is partly anticipated by prior work the paper itself cites (e.g., Yue et al., Wang et al. on RL not introducing fundamentally new reasoning abilities). The paper acknowledges the closed-source comparison is confounded by lack of transparency (footnote 3), so the asymmetry should be stated more cautiously.

The paper claims the benchmark evaluates fine-grained visual understanding, but it does not isolate what aspect of visual understanding fails (e.g., reading text labels vs. spatial topology). The no-input ablation is helpful but coarse; a targeted analysis (e.g., text-only station list vs. map image) would strengthen the claim that visual perception specifically is the bottleneck.
Geographic/linguistic coverage is moderate (30 cities, 13 countries) and skewed toward a subset of languages; the paper acknowledges this, but it limits generality claims.

strengths: Introduces ReasonMap, a benchmark for fine-grained visual reasoning from high-resolution transit maps, with 1,008 question-answer pairs spanning 30 cities in 13 countries; it complements existing benchmarks by jointly evaluating fine-grained visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and route planning.

Provides a semi-automated, semi-scalable construction pipeline with data collection, question generation, reference-route collection, annotation, and quality control, including manual verification, difficulty balancing, and detailed documentation in the supplementary material.

Proposes a two-level evaluation framework that separates answer correctness (accuracy) from answer quality (map score), with fine-grained components such as route name, departure/arrival stops, transfer consistency, via-stop count, and IoU-based via-stop matching.

Reports extensive experiments on 16 MLLMs, including base vs. reasoning models, open-source vs. closed-source models, visual-masking settings, language ablation, symbolic-map representation, and systematic error analysis, yielding useful insights into current MLLM limitations.
Establishes a GRPO-based reinforcement-learning baseline on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B that improves accuracy and map score while reducing token usage, providing a reproducible reference for future work.
The paper is clearly written, well-illustrated, and supported by extensive appendices, public implementation details, source links, and licensing information, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark's question diversity is limited: only one short-question template and two long-question templates are used, all asking for a route between two stops; this may not fully capture the breadth of fine-grained visual reasoning or planning, and the dataset size (1,008 QA pairs, 312 test samples) is modest.

The evaluation metrics are largely heuristic and not fully validated: map-score weights are hand-designed, correctness requires strict output format and can conflate format compliance with reasoning, and there is no human or upper-bound validation of the map score.

The headline finding that open-source reasoning models underperform their base counterparts is not rigorously supported by controlled comparisons across most models; only the Kimi-VL-A3B pair is same-family, while other comparisons confound architecture, training data, and scale, so the claim is overgeneralized.

The GRPO training baseline is limited to two Qwen2.5-VL models and lacks comparisons to supervised fine-tuning or other RL algorithms, making claims about consistent improvement and training efficacy preliminary.

Potential data contamination and reliance on prior knowledge are not fully ruled out: the transit maps and station names may appear in pretraining data, and text-only/symbolic experiments show models can exploit non-visual priors; the paper cannot quantify this contamination.

Ground-truth routes are collected from external map APIs and may not always match the visual map; although manual correction is applied, the final ground-truth error rate and coverage are not rigorously quantified.
The domain is narrow: transit-map reasoning may not generalize to other visual reasoning tasks, which the authors acknowledge but still limits the benchmark's broader impact.
No human performance or simple OCR/rule-based baseline is provided to calibrate task difficulty and contextualize the reported model accuracies.

strengths: Introduces ReasonMap, a novel high-resolution transit-map benchmark targeting fine-grained visual reasoning, spatial reasoning, and route planning, filling a gap left by benchmarks focused on symbolic/mathematical reasoning or coarse map understanding.

The dataset is carefully constructed via a semi-automated pipeline with manual quality control, covering 30 high-resolution transit maps from 13 countries, two question types and three templates, difficulty labels, and reference routes; the high resolution (avg ~5,839 x 5,449) and multilingual nature make it a useful resource.

Proposes a two-level evaluation framework that measures both answer correctness (accuracy) and answer quality (map score), with detailed scoring algorithms and difficulty-aware weighting, enabling more nuanced assessment than binary accuracy alone.

Conducts extensive experiments on 16 MLLMs, including visual-masking, symbolic/text-only, language-ablation, OCR-correlation, and error analyses, yielding useful insights about visual grounding versus language priors and about open-source versus closed-source reasoning models.

Provides a reproducible GRPO-based RL training baseline that improves performance, with public implementation details, prompts, and templates in the appendix, supporting future research on visual reasoning.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is modest: 1,008 QA pairs with only 312 test samples across 30 maps; some difficulty buckets contain very few samples (e.g., 1 sample for hard-middle), limiting statistical power and the strength of generalization claims.

The benchmark scope is limited to static transit maps, so the findings may not transfer directly to other fine-grained visual reasoning domains; the authors acknowledge this but it still restricts the broader impact of the conclusions.

Evaluation relies heavily on rule-based string matching and hand-designed score weights; despite sensitivity analysis and formatting corrections, semantically correct alternative routes or stylistic variations may still be penalized, and human validation of the proposed map score is limited.

Dataset construction uses MLLM-based extraction followed by manual correction (initial error rate reported around 16%), so residual annotation noise is possible; reference routes collected from external APIs may also not always align perfectly with the visual map.

Some headline findings (e.g., open-source base models outperforming reasoning variants) may be confounded by output-format adherence, token length, language bias, and differences in training data composition; closed-source comparisons also lack full transparency, as the authors note.
The training baseline covers only Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B with GRPO and does not compare against SFT or other RL variants, making the baseline preliminary rather than a comprehensive reference.
Algorithm 2's notation for capping the map score appears ambiguous or garbled in the manuscript, which could hinder reproducibility and should be clarified.

strengths: Transit maps are a reasonable and underexplored domain for probing visual reasoning, and the paper correctly observes that many existing map benchmarks (e.g., MapEval, GeoNav) bypass genuine visual grounding by relying on external tools or symbolic input. The proposed benchmark explicitly forbids tool use, which is a sensible design choice.

The dataset construction pipeline is documented in unusual detail, including a quality-control step with three domain experts, a reported ~16% initial error rate, manual correction, and difficulty balancing. This level of transparency is better than typical for benchmark papers.

The two-level evaluation framework (correctness/accuracy plus a quality-oriented 'map score') is a reasonable attempt to distinguish 'did the model get the right answer' from 'is the answer well-formed and well-supported,' and the appendix provides concrete algorithms (Algorithms 1 and 2) for both.

The evaluation covers 16 MLLMs across open- and closed-source families, and the visual-masking experiment (Table 3) is a genuinely useful probe: it quantifies how much each model actually depends on the image versus language priors, and shows that some models degrade dramatically without the map.

The error analysis (Figure 3, Appendix C.5/D) is concrete and well-illustrated, with real examples of visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, and refusal, and it helpfully distinguishes OCR failures from grounding and spatial-reasoning failures.
weaknesses: Task diversity is far narrower than the 'fine-grained visual reasoning' framing implies. Every question is essentially 'how do I get from Stop 1 to Stop 2' rendered in one short and two long templates that differ mainly in output format (count via stops vs. enumerate via stops). This is a single task type (transit route planning) dressed up as a broad reasoning benchmark, which substantially limits the generality of any conclusions and the usefulness of the benchmark beyond pathfinding.

The scale is small for a benchmark contribution: 1,008 total QA pairs and only 312 test samples, drawn from 30 maps. Several difficulty buckets are extremely thin (the paper reports only 1 sample for the hard-middle pair and 7 for hard-hard in Figure A1), so many of the 'difficulty-aware' comparisons rest on a handful of items.

The proposed metrics are ad hoc. The 'map score' assigns arbitrary point values (1 for endpoints, 2 for route name, 1 each for departure/arrival stops, cap at 10 or 40), the difficulty-weight matrix (1.0–3.0) is hand-tuned, and the num_via_stop_score and via_stop_score formulas use ad hoc constants (e.g., 4−error, scaling by 10). There is no validation that these scores correlate with human judgments of answer quality, so treating them as a principled measure of 'quality' is not supported.

Correctness is evaluated under a strict format requirement, and answers that cannot be parsed are marked wrong. Table 2 shows the 'weighted accuracy' numbers are heavily format-dependent; a model can know the correct route but be scored as failing for stylistic deviation. This conflates instruction-following/format compliance with visual reasoning ability, and the headline accuracy numbers should be interpreted with this caveat.

The central comparison between base and reasoning models is confounded. The open-source 'reasoning' models (Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking, Skywork-R1V, QvQ) come from different families, sizes, and training pipelines than the base models, and the closed-source reasoning models are evaluated via opaque APIs. The paper itself acknowledges in a footnote that the cross-source comparison 'may not be fair due to lack of transparency,' yet still draws strong conclusions (e.g., that RL causes 'visual confusion' and repeated trial-and-verification failures). These causal claims are not supported by the evidence presented.

The 'counterintuitive' headline finding (base models outperforming reasoning-tuned variants on some benchmarks) is already documented in the literature, including reference [89] which the authors cite ('Does reinforcement learning really incentivize reasoning capacity'). Framing this as a novel discovery overstates the originality of the analysis.

Ground-truth ambiguity is not adequately addressed. Transit maps admit multiple valid routes, and the benchmark defines correctness against a single route retrieved from Google/Gaode APIs. The paper mentions collecting multiple reference routes and taking the best score, but the correctness algorithm (Algorithm 1) checks against a single canonical route, so legitimate alternative routes can be marked incorrect. Reproducibility is also at risk because reference routes depend on external APIs that change over time.

Novelty relative to prior map benchmarks is not clearly established. MapEval, MapBench, CityBench, and MapLM are cited and dismissed as either tool-dependent or coarse-grained, but the concrete technical distinction between REASONMAP and these works (beyond 'no tools' and 'high resolution') is thin, and the paper does not empirically compare against them.

The GRPO training baseline is weak as a contribution: only two models (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B) are trained, and the resulting scores remain far below larger baselines. It is presented as one of four main contributions, but it functions more as a small pilot experiment than as a demonstrated training recipe.

The dataset difficulty distribution is skewed (57.7% easy, 34.4% medium, 7.8% hard), and the language-bias finding (Appendix C.3, English vs. Chinese station names) suggests that map/station-name language is a significant confound in the benchmark that is not controlled for in the main results.
